choices.text: The probability that the null hypothesis is true is 3%
If the null were true, 3% of experiments would give data this extreme
The probability that the alternative hypothesis is true is 3%

questions.feedback: That trap reading is the one to unlearn: A p-value of 0.03 means there is a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true. Reteach point: The p-value is about the data given the null: if H0 were true, 3% of experiments would give data this extreme.
questions.misconception: A p-value of 0.03 means there is a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true.
questions.prompt: A hypothesis test returns a p-value of 0.03. What does the 0.03 actually measure?

questions.answer: 1. The standard deviation of the sample mean is sigma / root n = 10 / root 100 = 10 / 10 = 1.
questions.feedback: The sampling distribution of the mean keeps the population mean but shrinks the spread by root n. If you divided by 100 instead of root 100 you shrank too far - the shrink is by root n, never by n itself.
questions.prompt: A population has standard deviation 10. Find the standard deviation of the sample mean for samples of size n = 100, and state the rule you used.

choices.text: Accept the null, because 0.012 is a small number
Reject the null, because 0.012 is smaller than alpha = 0.05
No verdict is possible without knowing the sample size

questions.feedback: The verdict is p against alpha: 0.012 < 0.05, so the data is surprising enough under the null to reject it. Small p means reject - anchor on the comparison with alpha, not on the size of the number alone.
questions.prompt: A test at the 5% level returns a p-value of 0.012. What is the correct verdict?

questions.answer: A Type I error - a false alarm. Its probability is capped by the significance level alpha.
questions.feedback: Rejecting a true null is a Type I error, the false alarm, and alpha is chosen in advance to cap how often it can happen. The other error, accepting a false null, is Type II - the missed signal.
questions.prompt: A fire-alarm test wrongly rejects a true null hypothesis and triggers an evacuation when there is no fire. Name this type of error, and state the quantity that caps its probability.
